chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
title: Hearing arrangements in his head: why his charts were called hard
summary: He denies writing hard music for its own sake, describes hearing a whole band in his head, and says his eyesight now limits his arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You had a reputation for writing hard music.

Well, I don't know why they were saying my music was hard. The same way when I had those three kids when we had the Happy Pappy television show, and the boy came down and he saw me, and he says, Randolph, you don't know me, but I know you. I lost a job on account of your arrangements. I couldn't play your arrangements one time. I didn't know whether to start ducking or not.
But, no, I don't write arrangements just to be making arrangements hard.
I write -- yeah, just what I hear. I hear, and I place it and I can see it like -- you teach percussion, don't you?
And I know at a time you could just close your ears and you can just hear them all around you. You can hear those beats.

Yeah. Now, that's what happens. That's what happens with me with an arrangement. I make arrangements -- I sit down, I take a score, piece of music, and I'll look at it. And I'll start the -- and all at once, all in this room, its
just filled with -- and I can just hear. And if you're on the outside looking at me, you'd say, that guy is nuts, because I'm laughing at what I hear.
At what you hear in your head.
In my head. And it's funny. The sound is good, and I'm going (musical sounds).
Not too much. I want to, but this is kind of hampering.
Because I got my magnifying glass, I got all kinds of magnifying glasses here.
